turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on through, Derek, and you too, Sandra. It's only the repeat review, nothing scary. How have you been getting on?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. Completely fine. Bit of a waste of an appointment, if I'm honest. The chemist just said the repeats were running out.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Don't let him brush you off. He's been hobbling round the kitchen, and he told me to ask you for a stronger painkiller.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I said the paracetamol was a bit useless. I didn't say I was hobbling. It's a niggle, Sandra, not a crisis.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): A niggle's still allowed to be talked about. What's the knee actually doing, day to day?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Right knee. Dull ache if I sit too long, stiff when I first get up, then I walk it off. Nothing to write home about.
[SEG0007] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He is writing home about it, sort of. He's up in the night with it, rubbing the knee, three times this week.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the loo, not the knee. I sleep fine. Once a night for a wee, which is normal at sixty-eight, and then I'm out like a light.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): So I'm hearing two stories about the nights. I'll park that. How long has this particular ache been grumbling?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): The wear and tear is years. This little patch, about three weeks. Still minor.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, three weeks. He was alright before the cold snap. Both knees have the arthritis, but it's the right one complaining.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): You've been told it's osteoarthritis, haven't you?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Years ago, both knees. They did keyhole on the left, must be ten years back, and left the right alone. Hips are fine, I'm not falling apart.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Before we look at the slip, what are you actually taking, in your own words?

[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, paracetamol, two of the five-hundred tablets, four times a day. Naproxen twice a day. Amlodipine for the blood pressure. Atorvastatin at night for the cholesterol. And the stomach one, lansoprazole, in the morning. I think that's the lot.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lovely. Sandra, would you read me what the pharmacy list says?

[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Paracetamol five hundred milligrams, two tablets four times a day. Naproxen two hundred and fifty milligrams, one twice a day. Lansoprazole thirty milligrams every morning. Amlodipine five milligrams once a day. Atorvastatin twenty milligrams at night.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The naproxen's wrong. I take five hundred milligrams, not two fifty. Twice a day, breakfast and with my tea, the big tablets. Always have.
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm looking at the box as well, Derek. It says two hundred and fifty. You've not been on five hundred.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Then they've changed it behind my back. I'm still sure it was five hundred. Well, actually, fairly sure.

[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to adjudicate without the packet in my hand, and you've each got a different strength. Twice a day we agree on. The dose stays unconfirmed, and I won't rewrite the naproxen today.
[SEG0022] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So which one does he swallow this evening?
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Whatever is printed on the box at home. If you ring the chemist this afternoon and ask what they last dispensed, that'll settle it. Bring the box next time either way.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. It's hardly the end of the world. I forget the names of the blooming things half the time anyway.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): The lansoprazole, thirty milligrams, every morning, or a bit hit and miss?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Hit and miss, if I'm honest. Most mornings. If I haven't got heartburn I sometimes just don't bother.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The packet barely moves. He skips it half the week, I've watched him.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you're on the naproxen it's worth taking even when your tummy feels quiet. Any burning in the chest, or black, tarry stools?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): The allotment's coming on, tomatoes are in. And the stairs at home are no trouble at all these days.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm glad the stairs are behaving, and good luck with the tomatoes. I was asking about your stomach, though. Any heartburn, or stools that look black?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No heartburn, no black stools. Tummy's been completely fine. Don't know why we keep on about it.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Because naproxen can irritate the stomach, that's all. Any dizziness with the amlodipine, or swollen ankles?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No dizziness. Ankles get a bit puffy if I've stood at the allotment all afternoon. That's just being sixty-eight. Barely worth a mention.
[SEG0034] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Barely worth a mention if you don't look down. Sock marks every evening, both ankles.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll have a look in a minute. And the statin, any muscle aches that feel different from the knee?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Muscles are fine. It's only that knee, and even that isn't bad.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): What settles the knee when it does ache, and what sets it off?

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Sitting too long sets it off, same story for the last three weeks. Walking it off helps, and a hot water bottle in the evening. The naproxen takes the edge off. Paracetamol doesn't do much, which is why I mentioned something stronger. Not that I actually need it.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): What did you have in mind, when you say stronger?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, co-codamol, or tramadol, um, whatever you usually give. I'm not desperate. It was only an idea, really.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He had tramadol up on his phone on the bus. He wants to keep digging the allotment, that's the truth of it.

[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can see why you'd ask. I'm not going to start co-codamol or tramadol, though. They can make you drowsy and constipated, and you're still driving. They won't mend the joint.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Knew you'd say that. Fair enough. It really is minor, however many times I have to say it.
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll say minor all the way home as well. Just ignore him.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do keep the paracetamol regular, two tablets four times a day, and don't go over eight tablets in the day. Take the naproxen with food, whichever strength is in the box. The hot water bottle and the little walks are exactly the right idea.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I already take the paracetamol like that. I'm not daft.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I know you're not. Any other illnesses for this review, diabetes, asthma, heart problems of your own?

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes, no asthma, no heart problems. Blood pressure for years, and they stuck me on the cholesterol tablet. That's the lot. Oh, my dad had a heart attack, but he was sixty-nine, so hardly young.
[SEG0049] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sixty-nine, yes. And you had that penicillin rash as a boy. You always pretend it wasn't an allergy.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): It wasn't an allergy. A tiny rash, years ago, and I'm not allergic to anything. Never have been.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll put down that you don't think you have an allergy, and that Sandra remembers a penicillin rash. I won't call it definite, but we'll keep penicillin off to be safe. Do you smoke at all, or drink much?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked. Couple of pints on a Saturday, that's all. Hardly counts.

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's straightforward. Before you came in we checked your blood pressure, one hundred and thirty-six over eighty-four, and your pulse was seventy-two. Both absolutely fine.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): There you are. Nothing wrong with me.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure's happy, yes. Let me see the ankles and that right knee.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Both ankles are mildly puffy, and they pit when I press. The right knee isn't warm and it isn't red. It bends all the way, and I can't feel any fluid in it.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Like I said. Normal knee. Puffy ankles that don't matter.

[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): I think this is a flare of the osteoarthritis in the right knee. It doesn't look like an infection or a clot. The ankle swelling is mild, and the amlodipine can add to it, so I won't stop that tablet today.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): A flare. That's the word. Hardly worth all this.

[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll reauthorise the paracetamol, lansoprazole thirty milligrams each morning, amlodipine five milligrams, and atorvastatin twenty at night, all unchanged. Naproxen stays on the repeat without me altering the strength. I'm also referring you to physiotherapy.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Physio if you insist. They'll just tell me to keep moving, which I already do. I still don't want a fuss.

[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): No fuss, and no co-codamol or tramadol from me. I'll see you in three months for the next repeat review, sooner if the knee blows up, goes hot, or you can't put weight on it. Sandra, if you can ring the chemist today, and mind how you go.
